transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi. Um, I guess I'm here because I've been having some trouble at work lately. I'm a hairstylist, and... well, my hands just feel like they’re moving through glue. 

Like, even doing the basic stuff, like sectioning hair or mixing color, it just takes me forever now. It's getting to the point where my coworkers and people at the salon have started noticing that I’m just a lot slower than I used to be. So, I figured I should come in and talk to somebody about it.
When you're doing these tasks with your hands, do you notice any shaking or trembling, or does it feel more like your hands are just weak or tired?

Um, no, they don't shake or tremble at all. And I wouldn't really say they feel weak, exactly. It's more just... like I was saying, that heavy, sluggish feeling. Like there's actual resistance when I try to move them. My brain knows how to do the normal motions, but my hands just won't move at their normal speed, so everything just takes a lot more effort and time to get through.
Besides the slowness in your hands, have you noticed any difficulty with your balance, or do you find yourself moving more slowly overall—like when you're walking or getting up from a chair?

Um, my balance is fine, I haven't noticed any problems with that. And as for walking or getting up... I don't really think I'm moving slower overall. 

Like I mentioned, it really just feels like it's my hands at work. That's where it's the most obvious, when I'm trying to section hair or mix the color and it just takes me forever. That's what people at the salon are noticing—just that I'm a lot slower at doing those specific things than I used to be.
When you try to move your hands, do they feel stiff or rigid, or does it feel more like you're just moving through resistance without the stiffness?

Um, no, they don't really feel stiff or rigid. It's not like my joints are locked up or anything. It's just... like I said, it really does just feel like they're moving through glue. There's just this heavy resistance when I'm at work, and doing things like sectioning the hair or mixing the color just takes me forever now. It's just that slowness that everyone's noticing, not really a stiffness.
Over the past few weeks or months, have you been feeling sad, down, or depressed, or noticed changes in your mood or energy levels in general?

Yeah, I have. For the past few months, honestly. Most days, I just wake up with this... heavy, flat sadness right in my chest. It just sits there. It feels like... I don't know, like there's just no point in trying to build the life I was planning on having. It's just hard to care about much of anything right now.

When you're not at work—like at home, doing things around the house or in your free time—do you notice that same heavy, sluggish feeling in your hands, or is it really just something that happens when you're working at the salon?

Um... honestly, I don't really notice it much at home. It's really just at work. That's where it's the most obvious. Like I was saying, my hands just feel like they're moving through glue when I'm there. Even just the basic stuff, like sectioning hair or mixing color... it just takes me forever now. It's gotten to the point where people at the salon have actually started noticing that I'm just a lot slower than I used to be. But at home, no, it's not really like that.

When you're at work and you notice your hands feeling slow, does the slowness get worse when you're stressed or upset about something, or does it stay about the same regardless of how you're feeling emotionally at that moment?

Um, I don't think it really changes based on how I'm feeling. It's just kind of always there when I'm working. Like I said, it just feels like my hands are moving through glue. Whether I'm stressed or just having a normal day, sectioning the hair or mixing the color just takes me forever now. It stays pretty much the same, and that's why people at the salon have started noticing that I'm just slower than I used to be.

When you're at work and your hands feel slow, if you suddenly get really focused on something—like if a favorite customer came in and you were excited to do their hair—does that heavy, sluggish feeling in your hands go away or get better, or does it stay just as strong no matter what?

No, it doesn't really go away. Even if it's someone I really like, or a cut I usually enjoy doing... it doesn't matter. My hands still just feel like they're moving through glue. It's like my body just won't cooperate, no matter how I'm feeling about the appointment. I'm still just so slow at sectioning the hair and mixing the color, and it still takes me forever. Like I said, it's gotten bad enough that my coworkers have pointed out how much slower I am now. It just doesn't change.

When you're doing other things that require fine hand movements—like writing, eating with a fork, buttoning buttons, or texting on your phone—do your hands feel that same heavy, glue-like slowness, or is it really just limited to the hair styling tasks at work?

Um... no, it's really just at work. When I'm texting or eating, or doing stuff like that, I don't really notice it. It's just when I'm doing hair. Like I was saying, it's the sectioning and the mixing color where my hands just feel like they're moving through glue. That's what takes me forever, and that's what the other people at the salon are noticing. It's just... I'm just slower at my job now.
Before you came to see me today, did you go to your regular doctor or any other doctors about this heavy feeling in your hands and the slowness? And if so, what did they find or tell you?
No, I haven't seen any other doctors about it. You're the first person I've talked to about this. I just... I haven't gone anywhere else for it.

You mentioned feeling that heavy, flat sadness in your chest most mornings. When you wake up and feel that sadness, do you also notice your hands feeling slow and heavy at that moment, or does the hand slowness mainly start once you get to work?

Well, the sadness is definitely there in the morning. Most days, I wake up with this heavy, flat sadness in my chest... it just feels like there's no point in trying to build the life I was planning. But the slowness with my hands, I don't really notice that until I get to work and start trying to do hair. The sadness is what I wake up with.

You mentioned that your hands feel slow and heavy only when you're at work doing hair, but not when you're texting or eating at home. Have you ever noticed your hands feeling that same glue-like slowness during any other activities outside of work—like when you're getting ready in the morning, or doing anything else that requires fine hand movements?

No, it really is just at work. Like I said, getting ready in the morning, or doing other things... it's fine. It's just when I'm at the salon. My hands just feel like they're moving through glue when I'm there. Even sectioning hair or mixing color takes me forever now. That's why people at work have started noticing that I'm just slower than I used to be. But outside of work, no, I haven't noticed it with anything else.

When you're at home in the evening after work, do you feel physically tired or fatigued in general, or do you feel like your whole body is just slow and heavy—like even simple movements feel like they take more effort than they should?

Um, no, not really. I mean, I get tired after work just from being on my feet all day, but my whole body doesn't feel slow or heavy. Moving around at home is fine, it doesn't take extra effort. It really is just my hands when I'm at the salon. I don't feel that overall heaviness when I'm just at home in the evening.

When you're at home or doing things outside of work, have you noticed that activities that normally wouldn't take much time—like getting dressed, washing dishes, or tidying up—seem to take you longer than they used to, even if you don't think about your hands specifically?

Um, no, I haven't really noticed that. Getting dressed or washing dishes, things like that... they don't seem to take me any longer than they used to. I just do them at my normal pace. It really is just when I'm at the salon trying to do hair that things seem to take forever.

When you're at work at the salon, if you were to time yourself doing the same hair styling tasks—like sectioning or mixing color—compared to how long those exact same tasks took you before you started feeling this way, how much longer do they take you now? Are we talking about 10-20% slower, or is it much more significant than that?

Um, it's definitely a lot more than 10 or 20 percent. It's pretty significant. Like I was saying, it literally feels like my hands are moving through glue when I'm doing those tasks. So, you know, sectioning a client's hair or mixing the color in the back... it just takes me forever now. 

If something used to take me twenty or thirty minutes, it's taking me like forty-five or an hour now. It's noticeable enough that the other stylists have started pointing it out and asking if I'm okay. So... yeah, it's a lot slower than I used to be.
Have you been feeling anxious or worried about anything at work—like concerns about your job performance, relationships with coworkers, or anything else that's been stressing you out at the salon?

Um, well, yeah, actually. I have been pretty stressed out about things there. I know it sounds strange to say, but... I'm pretty sure someone at the salon has been watching my bookings and messing with my hours on purpose. It's just that the really slow days always seem to happen right after I talk out loud about needing to save money. So, yeah, that's definitely been worrying me a lot.

When you say someone at the salon has been watching your bookings and messing with your hours on purpose, have you actually seen them do this, or is this something you've concluded based on the pattern you've noticed with the slow days happening after you mention needing money?

I haven't seen them physically do it, like standing at the computer or whatever. But I just know it's happening. I mean, it's too much of a coincidence, right? Every single time I mention out loud that I need to save up for something or that money is tight, my schedule suddenly clears out for the next few days. It's like they're listening and then deliberately going in and messing with my hours to make sure I don't make any money. I know it sounds strange when I say it out loud, but I'm just pretty sure someone is doing it on purpose.

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with depressed mood (heavy, flat sadness in chest most mornings), anhedonia (hard to care about much), and functional impairment at work lasting several months. The hand slowness is work-specific, does not occur with other fine motor tasks, and persists regardless of emotional state or distraction—consistent with functional neurological symptom disorder (conversion disorder) rather than primary motor pathology. However, the prominent depressive symptoms, combined with work-specific somatic complaint and emerging ideas of reference (belief coworkers are deliberately manipulating her schedule), best fit Major Depressive Disorder with somatic features. The hand slowness appears to be a depressive manifestation rather than an independent neurological condition.
